title: DORA Metrics: Measuring How Well You Deliver
intro: Years of research across thousands of teams (the DORA programme) found four measures that track how well a team delivers software, and found that speed and stability go together: good teams have both. Two measure throughput and two measure stability. You can compute rough versions from data you already have. You're in the checkout service's repository; deploys are done by the workflow deploy.yml.

steps.prompt: Deployment frequency: count the successful runs of the deploy.yml workflow since 1 September 2026.
expected_commands: gh run list --workflow deploy.yml --status success --created ">2026-09-01" --json createdAt | jq length
gh run list --workflow deploy.yml --status success --created '>2026-09-01' --json createdAt | jq length
gh run list --workflow deploy.yml --status success --created ">2026-09-01" --json createdAt --limit 500 | jq length
gh run list --workflow=deploy.yml --status=success --created=">2026-09-01" --json createdAt | jq length
steps.hint: gh run list --workflow deploy.yml --status success --created ">2026-09-01" --json createdAt | jq length
steps.explanation: 62 production deploys in about a month: roughly three per working day.
steps.why: Deployment frequency measures batch size indirectly. Deploying often means each deploy is small, and a small change is easier to review, test, and roll back, and is easier to blame when something breaks. Teams that deploy rarely aren't being careful; they're shipping big, risky bundles.

steps.prompt: Lead time for changes: fetch the creation and merge times of pull requests merged since 1 September 2026, up to 200 of them.
steps.explanation: Half of changes merge within 21 hours; one in ten waits six days or more.
steps.why: Lead time is from a change being written to it running in production. The gap between median and 90th percentile is where to look: those slow changes are usually waiting for review, or are large. Measure to production, not just to merge, if deploys aren't automatic: a merged change that waits a week for a release train has a week of lead time.

steps.prompt:
Change failure rate. Of the 62 deploys, 5 were followed by a rollback or a hotfix. What's the change failure rate, and is it a concern?
  a) 5%, excellent
  b) About 8%, which is in the healthy range; the aim isn't zero, it's cheap and fast recovery
  c) 62%, terrible
  d) It can't be calculated
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
5 failed / 62 deploys = 8.1%

a rate of 0% over a long period usually means: very few deploys, or failures that aren't being recorded
steps.explanation: 8%: a few deploys in every hundred need fixing.
steps.why: Some changes will fail; a team that never has a failed change is either barely changing anything or not counting. What matters is that failures are small and quickly undone, which is the fourth metric. Count honestly: a rollback, a hotfix, or an incident caused by a deploy all count, and people have to feel safe reporting them.

steps.prompt:
Time to restore service: how long from a failure starting to users being served again. Which of these most reduces it?
  a) A longer approval process before each deploy
  b) Fast detection and a rollback that's one tested, routine action
  c) Deploying only on Tuesdays
  d) Larger releases
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
time to restore = time to detect + time to decide + time to roll back
  detect   : alerts on user-facing symptoms          (minutes, not a customer email)
  decide   : 'roll back first, diagnose after'       (no meeting)
  roll back: automated, practised on every deploy    (seconds to minutes)
steps.hint: Break the time into its parts.
steps.explanation: See it quickly, and have an undo that always works.
steps.why: Approval gates add lead time and, according to the same research, don't reduce failures; they increase batch size, which makes failures worse. The teams that recover in minutes are the ones that can roll back without thinking. This is where the two halves meet: small frequent deploys are what make fast recovery possible.

steps.prompt:
Management wants to set each team a target for these four numbers and rank the teams. What's the risk?
  a) None: targets improve everything
  b) A measure that becomes a target gets gamed: tiny meaningless deploys to raise frequency, failures left unrecorded. Use the metrics for a team to see its own trend, not to rank teams
  c) The numbers are secret
  d) Teams will deploy less
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
useful   : 'our lead time doubled this quarter: why?'   (a team reading its own trend)
harmful  : 'team A deploys 3x more than team B'          (different systems, incentive to game)
steps.explanation: Use them as a mirror for each team, not a league table.
steps.why: The four metrics are symptoms of how work flows; pushing on the numbers directly bends the reporting instead of the work. A payments system and a marketing site shouldn't have the same deployment frequency. Used well, they point a team at its own bottleneck, review queues, slow tests, a manual release step, and show whether fixing it helped.
